Global Markets Brief
Dear Investor,
This week, we look at how the US is tightening its grip on China's access to advanced AI chips and how this is reshaping the global semiconductor industry. We also examine the widening US-China computing gap, the correction in Chinese chip stocks and the growing opportunities for alternative chipmakers as competition in the AI sector intensifies.

Technology · Semiconductors
The Battle for AI Chips Is Heating Up
The AI race is moving beyond chip manufacturing. The US is tightening China’s access to advanced computing, China is trying to reduce its dependence on foreign technology, and investors are reassessing which companies will benefit from the next phase of AI infrastructure spending.
China’s Growing Reliance on Overseas Computing
China’s access to advanced AI computing increasingly depends on infrastructure outside its borders. The chart estimates that by the end of 2027, 32% of China’s AI compute could come through remote access to overseas data centres, while another 7% could come from chip smuggling. Together, these channels could account for nearly 40% of its computing capacity. By comparison, 36% is estimated to come from capacity already in China, with future domestic production contributing 18%.
Source: Institute for Progress (via Bloomberg)
This dependence has made Southeast Asia an important part of China’s AI ecosystem. Chinese technology companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, have reportedly accessed advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centres, including facilities in Malaysia and Singapore. This has allowed them to rent computing power without directly importing restricted processors, creating a loophole that Washington is now seeking to close.
Washington Tightens Control Over Access to AI Chips
The US has introduced new licensing rules to restrict Chinese access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centres, particularly in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. The focus is shifting from controlling chip shipments to monitoring who ultimately uses the computing power. The rules could increase compliance costs and uncertainty for Southeast Asian data centres serving Chinese clients. However, the region’s wider semiconductor exports may remain supported by demand from US technology companies, making the impact uneven across businesses.
The US-China Gap in AI Computing Capacity
Source: Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker), X
The chart shows the US-China AI computing gap widening from 2.8x in 2023 to 5.9x in 2025, with the ratio projected to reach 14.1x by 2027. Nvidia, alongside Google, Amazon and AMD, accounts for a large share of US capacity, while China relies on domestic suppliers such as Huawei. Tighter US restrictions could slow China’s access to advanced chips in the near term, but may accelerate investment in domestic alternatives. Greater usage of local chips could help Chinese developers improve their hardware, optimise AI software and strengthen the domestic semiconductor ecosystem over time.
China’s Chip Stocks Lose Momentum as Restrictions Intensify
Chinese AI chip stocks have lost much of their earlier gains as investors worry that tighter US restrictions could make it harder for domestic designers to access overseas manufacturing facilities. Speculation around Samsung reviewing its Chinese chipmaking customers added to the selling pressure.
Source: Bloomberg (November 2026)
The correction also reflects high valuations. Cambricon, Hygon and Moore Threads were still trading at over 45 times forward earnings, compared with around 14 times for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. Investors are therefore reassessing both the growth outlook and the prices they are willing to pay for these companies.
Investment in Specialised Semiconductor Companies Is Rising
Venture capital investment in specialised semiconductor companies has grown from around $1 billion in 2016 to approximately $25 billion in 2026 year to date. This reflects growing interest in chips designed for specific AI workloads, which can improve computing efficiency and reduce costs.
Source: PitchBook (via Financial Times)
This is creating opportunities for alternative suppliers such as AMD, Google and Amazon, alongside emerging European chip start-ups. However, commercial adoption remains uncertain, as developing and manufacturing advanced chips can take years.
US and Chinese Technology Stocks Diverge
Chinese technology stocks initially outperformed the Nasdaq 100 in 2026 but reversed sharply in the final quarter. Both markets have faced pressure amid concerns over AI valuations and the sustainability of heavy technology spending, but the SSE Star 50 has fallen more sharply, reflecting additional concerns around US export restrictions and China’s access to advanced chips.
Source: Financial Times / LSEG
US companies continue to benefit from established AI infrastructure and chip ecosystems, while Chinese firms face greater uncertainty over technology access. However, domestic semiconductor suppliers could benefit from Beijing’s push for greater technological self-reliance.
Why It Matters
The AI investment cycle is increasingly shaped by geopolitics, computing access and semiconductor competition. While US chipmakers retain an advantage, restrictions could accelerate China’s domestic alternatives and create opportunities for other suppliers. Investors should focus on companies with strong technology, sustainable demand and reasonable valuations, as rising AI spending will not benefit every semiconductor company equally.
